It is git under the hood: mise keeps its own repo and makes the commits for you, so day to day you don't run git yourself.

**How it works**
- History lives in a bare repo at `~/.local/state/mise/history/repo.git`, on branch `main`.
- Each checkpoint is one commit. Files are stored under `home/…` (for example `home/.config/hypr/…`), and mise's own config goes under `config/…`. Another machine restores them under its own home directory.
- The watcher service (`dev.mise.mise-history`) commits edits on its own once a file has been quiet for a short while.
- Once the origin is reconnected, it pushes those commits to GitHub, and fetches and pulls changes made on other machines. mise never force-pushes.
- You can read the repo with plain git, for example `GIT_DIR=~/.local/state/mise/history/repo.git git log`. Don't commit to it by hand; let mise do the writing.

**Day to day: nothing.** Edit configs as usual and they get saved. When you need something:

| Want to | Command |
|---|---|
| See state, unsaved changes, watcher health | `mise dot status` |
| See what changed | `mise dot history`, `mise dot history diff --patch` |
| Mark a known-good point | `mise dot save --description "..."` |
| Undo a bad edit | `mise dot rollback <path>` (and `mise dot undo` to reverse that) |
| See what an update changed | `mise dot capture --label omarchy-update -- omarchy-update` |
| Push or pull now instead of waiting | `mise dot sync`, `mise dot pull` |

**Upkeep**
- **Before tracking a new directory,** run `mise dot track --dry-run <dir>` or `mise dot paths --preview <dir>` first. The credential filter only goes by file name, and it missed your keys and tokens today. Exclude anything secret before the first save. If a secret does get saved, it stays in history (see the next point).
- **Nothing is ever deleted.** Checkpoints never expire and are never compacted, and untracking a file doesn't remove its old versions. Deleting a leaked secret from history means rewriting it, which `encryption.md` covers ("Remove plaintext from history").
- **Files that change constantly** get saved less often. `mise dot paths --noisy` lists them; `fish_variables` is the likely one. Either exclude them or track them with `--no-autosave` and save by hand.
- **Health checks:** `mise doctor` and `mise dot status` show a stopped watcher or failing saves or syncs. After a mise upgrade, run `mise bootstrap services apply` to restart the watcher on the new version.
- **Real secrets** go in with `encrypt = true` (age recipients), or into fnox (item 4), rather than being excluded.

**How the other git repos fit in**
- `~/.config/skogai`, `~/.config/containers/systemd`, `~/.skogai` and `/skogai` stay normal git repos: you commit and push them yourself. mise skips them as nested repos, and `[bootstrap.repos]` clones them on a new machine.

input.last_assistant_message:
The mise MCP is thin. In practice it's a safety map plus two narrow actions, and almost everything real still goes through Bash.

**What it has**

| Piece | What it does in practice |
|---|---|
| `list_commands` | A catalog of every mise command (~200), each labelled `read`, `write` or `destructive`. It can't run anything. This is the most useful part. |
| `install_tool` | Installs a tool version. Narrow, and the same as `mise install`/`use`. |
| `run_task` | Runs a mise task. Since a task can contain any code, this is "run arbitrary code" with extra steps. Only one task is defined here (the guarded `bootstrap` task). |
| `mise://tools`, `tasks`, `config` | Read-only snapshots, roughly the same as `mise ls`, `tasks ls` and `config ls`. |
| `mise://env` | The resolved environment. It can contain secrets, so don't read it without asking (as `mise.md` already says). |

There's no MCP tool for `bootstrap`, `dotfiles`, `doctor`, `outdated` or the rest, so all of those go through Bash anyway.

**How far to trust the labels**

They're mostly sensible, but "read" means the command changes no state, not that it's safe to run:

- `token github`/`gitlab`/`forgejo` are labelled `read`, but they print a token. `env` is `read` too and can show secrets.
- Parent commands take the label of their worst subcommand. `settings`, `vars` and `deps` show as `write` even when they only list. `dotfiles origin` shows as `destructive` even when it only shows the origin. `bootstrap` with no subcommand is `destructive` because it runs the full apply.
- `run`, `exec`, `watch`, `en`, `dotfiles capture` and `daemons start/stop` have no label at all, so they need confirmation.

**Verdict:** worth keeping for the classification, which backs the "read freely, confirm write/destructive" rule in `mise.md`'s session protocol. As a way to drive mise it adds almost nothing over Bash.

I could add the "read ≠ safe" exception (token, env) to the MCP section of `mise.md`. Want that?

# Atuin

Atuin (https://atuin.sh) is installed and is Emil's primary way of both
storing shell history and managing environment variables/aliases across
machines. This is a living record of that setup, updated directly as the
agreement changes — not derived from any single dotfiles file.

## What it does here

- **Shell history sync.** Every command run in an interactive shell is
  recorded and synced to Emil's atuin.sh account (username `skogix`), so
  history is shared across machines.
- **Env vars and aliases.** New environment variables and shell aliases are
  added via Atuin's dotfiles feature, not hand-written into `.bashrc`/`.zshrc`,
  so they sync to every machine automatically:
  - `atuin dotfiles var set NAME=value` — add/update an env var
  - `atuin dotfiles var delete NAME` — remove one
  - `atuin dotfiles var list` — see what's set
  - `atuin dotfiles alias set name=command` — add/update an alias
  - `atuin dotfiles alias delete name` / `list` / `clear` — same idea

  belong directly in shell rc files instead.

# Containers: Docker → Podman

This is a living record of the container-runtime setup, updated directly as
the agreement changes — not derived from any single dotfiles file. It
documents a deliberate divergence from Omarchy's stock Docker setup, the same
way `window-manager.md` tracks divergence from Omarchy's default bindings.

## Why

Omarchy ships a full Docker environment by default: `docker`,
`docker-buildx`, `docker-compose`, `lazydocker`, `ufw-docker`, a `docker.socket`
enabled at boot, Docker-specific UFW rules, a `Super+Shift+D` TUI binding, a
Docker.desktop launcher, and menu entries — plus an opt-in (never used on this
machine) "Sudoless Docker" toggle that adds the user to the root-equivalent
`docker` group. Emil decided to move off Docker entirely in favor of Podman
(rootless by default, no always-on root daemon) rather than keep tuned the
sudoless-vs-sudo Docker tradeoff.

## What changes

- **Packages:** remove `docker`, `docker-compose`, `docker-buildx`,
  `ufw-docker`. Install `podman`, `podman-docker` (provides/conflicts with
  `docker` — this is what lets the `docker` command keep working, backed by
  Podman), `podman-compose`.
- **`lazydocker` stays installed.** It has no hard dependency on the `docker`
  package. It talks to the Docker Engine API at `$DOCKER_HOST`, which
  `podman-docker` points at the rootless Podman socket (see the systemd
  bullet), so it keeps working as long as `podman.socket` is enabled.
- **No changes needed to:** `~/.config/hypr` (`Super+Shift+D` binding),
  Docker.desktop launcher, Omarchy menu entries, or the `d=docker` atuin
  alias — all of them call `docker`, which keeps working.
- **systemd:** disable/stop `docker.socket`. Podman doesn't need an
  always-on root daemon. The `podman` CLI itself (`podman ps`, quadlets,
  `podman-compose`) is daemonless and reads container state directly, with
  no socket involved. Docker-API clients are different: lazydocker, Docker
  SDKs, and anything that mounts `docker.sock`. `podman-docker` ships
  `/etc/profile.d/podman-docker.sh`, which exports `DOCKER_HOST` to the
  rootless socket (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock`) for non-root
  users. So keep **`podman.socket` (user-level) enabled**. It starts
  `podman.service` on demand; don't enable the service itself (step 9).

# herdr

herdr (https://herdr.dev) is a terminal workspace manager for coding agents:
workspaces, tabs and panes, with agent state (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`,
`done`) recognised per pane. It is how skogai's agents get visible panes
and can drive each other. This page records the setup and the conventions
agreed for skogai; the binary's own `herdr --skill` is the authority on
command syntax.

## Per-machine setup

- Binary: `/usr/bin/herdr` (0.9.3 at time of writing). Server runs under
  the user; the socket is `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`.
- Config: `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`. It mirrors the Omarchy tmux config
  (`prefix = ctrl+space`, `prefix+c` new tab, `alt+h/j/k/l` focus). Apply
  changes with `herdr server reload-config`.
- Shell: `dash-skogai/fish/config.fish` loads `herdr completion fish`.
- Window manager: Omarchy's "Herdr" floating terminal is the dropdown
  terminal on `Mod+grave` (see `window-manager.md`).

## Agent integration

Claude Code reports pane state through a hook, installed by herdr:

- Hook: `~/.claude/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh`, a symlink directory to
  `/skogai/scripts/claude/hooks/`. The file is herdr-managed and is
  overwritten by `herdr integration install claude`.
- Settings: `~/.claude/settings.json` runs it with `session` on hooks.
- Check: `herdr integration status`. Upgrade the Claude hook with
  `herdr integration install claude` (v8 → v10 on 2026-10-07).

Other agents on this machine, as of the same check: pi and opencode are
outdated (`herdr integration install pi` / `opencode`); codex and hermes are
current; the rest are not installed.

## Conventions for skogai

- Agents act on herdr only from inside a herdr pane. The check is
  `test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1`. Outside herdr, do not control the focused
  session.

# mise

mise (https://mise.jdx.dev) is installed as the tool-version manager
(`~/.config/mise/config.toml`, 27 tools, all `latest`), with an Omarchy
layer at `/etc/mise/conf.d/omarchy.toml` (only a `cursor-agent` tool alias).
It is also wired up as an MCP server (`mise mcp`).

The build here (2026.10.9) does far more than manage tool versions. Several
of its features overlap with things this repo already handles another way
(atuin for env vars/aliases, hand-run steps in `containers.md`, etc.). This
page tracks a guided walk through those features, one at a time, to decide
for each one: adopt it, ignore it, or adopt it in place of something else.

## Session protocol

This walkthrough spans several sessions, with `/clear` in between. At the
start of each session:

1. If an item under **Walkthrough** is `[~]`, that's the current topic:
   read its notes and continue from there. Otherwise take the first item
   that isn't `[x]` (items can be taken out of order).
2. Run `mise <command> --help` for that topic (and `--help` on its
   subcommands as needed), then go through it with Emil: what it does, and
   how it relates to what's already in place on this machine.
3. Run only `read` subcommands (`status`, `ls`, `diff`, `plan`, ...)
   without asking. Confirm any `write` or `destructive` subcommand first.
   `mcp__mise__list_commands` gives the classification for each one.
4. Before ending, record the outcome under the topic's **Notes** (what was
   decided and why, what was changed) and update its marker:
   `[ ]` = not started, `[~]` = in progress, `[x]` = decided, `[-]` = skipped.

Don't read `mise env` or `mise://env` output into the conversation without
asking. It may contain secrets.

# Secrets: keys and who can read what

A living record of how secrets are encrypted and which user can decrypt
them, updated directly as the agreement changes. **Status: draft
(2026-10-14).** Nothing below has been created on the machine yet. The
mise side (how secrets reach `mise bootstrap` and tasks) is in `mise.md`,
item 4.

## Model

- Secrets are stored with fnox, encrypted with age. `fnox.toml` holds only
  ciphertext, so it is safe to commit and to share between users.
- A secret is encrypted to a list of **recipients** (public keys). Any one
  matching **identity** (private key) decrypts it.
- Separation between users comes from Linux file permissions on the
  identity files, not from fnox profiles. A profile only chooses which
  secrets get asked for.
- Trust goes one way: skogix (the admin, with sudo) can reach everything;
  agents can reach only their own keys.

## Keys

| File | Owner, mode | Created by | Leaves the machine | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `~skogix/.ssh/skogix-age.txt` | skogix, 0600 | skogix, once | Yes, carried like `id_rsa` | Personal and admin key: reads everything, enrols new keys |
| `~skogix/.ssh/local-per-machine-age.txt` | skogix, 0600 | bootstrap task, if missing | Never | skogix on this machine; revoke one machine on its own |
| `~claude/.ssh/local-per-machine-age.txt` | claude, 0600 | bootstrap task (as claude), if missing | Never | claude on this machine |

`~skogix/.ssh` and `~claude/.ssh` are 0700 and owned by their user. The
other agents (dot, amy, goose) follow the claude row when they need keys.

## Providers and profiles

Two fnox ideas that are easy to mix up (and were, in the Oct 11 tests):

- A **provider** decides how a secret is encrypted. For age that is the
  recipient list, so it decides **who can decrypt**. Providers are named
  after their readers.
- A **profile** decides **which secrets are asked for**. Profiles stack

# Window manager

This is a living record of the window-manager conventions Emil and Claude
have agreed on, updated directly as that agreement changes. It is not
derived from, or synced against, any single dotfiles config — if a machine's
actual config drifts from this file, that's a prompt to reconcile the two in

# mise

mise (https://mise.jdx.dev) is installed as the tool-version manager
(`~/.config/mise/config.toml`, 27 tools, all `latest`), with an Omarchy
layer at `/etc/mise/conf.d/omarchy.toml` (only a `cursor-agent` tool alias).
It is also wired up as an MCP server (`mise mcp`).

The build here (2026.10.9) does far more than manage tool versions. Several
of its features overlap with things this repo already handles another way
(atuin for env vars/aliases, hand-run steps in `containers.md`, etc.). This
page tracks a guided walk through those features, one at a time, to decide
for each one: adopt it, ignore it, or adopt it in place of something else.

## Session protocol

This walkthrough spans several sessions, with `/clear` in between. At the
start of each session:

1. If an item under **Walkthrough** is `[~]`, that's the current topic:
   read its notes and continue from there. Otherwise take the first item
   that isn't `[x]` (items can be taken out of order).
2. Run `mise <command> --help` for that topic (and `--help` on its
   subcommands as needed), then go through it with Emil: what it does, and
   how it relates to what's already in place on this machine.
3. Run only `read` subcommands (`status`, `ls`, `diff`, `plan`, ...)
   without asking. Confirm any `write` or `destructive` subcommand first.
   `mcp__mise__list_commands` gives the classification for each one.
4. Before ending, record the outcome under the topic's **Notes** (what was
   decided and why, what was changed) and update its marker:
   `[ ]` = not started, `[~]` = in progress, `[x]` = decided, `[-]` = skipped.

Don't read `mise env` or `mise://env` output into the conversation without
asking. It may contain secrets.

## MCP server

- Tools: `list_commands` (catalog with `read`/`write`/`destructive`
  labels; it can't run anything), `install_tool`, `run_task` (runs
  arbitrary task code).
- Resources: `mise://tools`, `mise://tasks`, `mise://env`, `mise://config`.
- Anything else (`ls`, `outdated`, `doctor`, `--help`, ...) still goes
  through Bash.

## Walkthrough

### [x] 1. `mise bootstrap` — declarative machine setup

Describes a whole machine in config and applies it.

- `status`, `plan` — read state / preview changes
- `packages` (`apply`, `status`, `use`, `upgrade`, `prune`, `import`,
  `export`, `brew tap/untap`, `where`) — system packages
- `services` (`apply`, `status`, `remove`) — services
- `linux systemd-units` (`apply`, `status`) — systemd user units
- `firewall` (`apply`, `status`) — host firewall
- `compose` (`apply`, `status`) — Compose projects
- `repos` (`apply`, `status`, `update`, `exec`) — git checkouts
- `files` (`apply`, `status`) — system files/directories
- `accounts` (`apply`, `status`) — Linux users/groups
- `user` (`apply`, `status`) — login shell
- `mise-shell-activate` (`apply`, `status`) — mise activation in shell rc
- `plugins` (`apply`, `status`) — package-manager plugins
- `secrets status` — whether declared secret inputs are available
- `remote` — bootstrap machines over SSH
- `unapply` — remove what bootstrap created
- (`macos ...` — not relevant here)

pacman/ufw/systemd steps in `containers.md` have been declared here instead?
Could the two compose stacks live under `[bootstrap.compose]`?

Notes:

- Picked ahead of item 2 (2026-10-14), straight after closing item 1.
  Nothing done yet: start with `mise secrets --help`,
  `mise bootstrap secrets --help`, `fnox --help` and
  `tmp/mise-docs/bootstrap/secrets.md`. Concrete cases from item 1: the
  cloudflared token (`/etc/cloudflared/token`, root 0600, hand-placed),
  gptme's `~/.config/gptme/server.env` (the `dev.mise.gptme-server`
  `environment_file`), and the API tokens cleared out of atuin vars on
  2026-09-30 (`atuin.md`).
- Two separate mechanisms (2026-10-14). References:
  `tmp/mise-docs/bootstrap/secrets.md`,
  `tmp/mise-docs/environments/secrets/fnox.md`, and the earlier tests in
  `tmp/mise-secrets-testing/` (who-and-mode example, gotchas). All
  tested with throwaway values, copies kept in the session scratchpad.
  - `[bootstrap.secrets]` names inputs (`name = "ENV_VAR"`) that
    `[bootstrap.files]` (`template = true`) and `[dotfiles]` templates read
    with `secret()`. It works from the global config and doesn't care
    where the values come from. Tested: `fnox exec -- mise bootstrap files
    apply` wrote a 0600 file. A rerun is `unchanged`, and after a rotated
    value (`fnox set`) the plan shows `update`. Without values, `plan`
    marks the file `unknown` ("required secret unavailable") and apply/
    dry-run stop before writing anything. `secrets status --missing` exits
    1. A `-v` apply log didn't contain the value.
  - `[secrets.fnox]` + task `secrets = [...]`: per-task grants. Only
    project `mise.toml` is read (global config is ignored), and tasks
    started by `mise bootstrap` can't receive secrets. The who-and-mode
    example still works on 2026.10.9: claude can't get `skogix-only`, the
    human can, `mise env` shows nothing.
  - Gotcha still present: a task with an identity that can't decrypt
    runs anyway, with empty values and exit 0. Fix: `if_missing =
    "error"` at the top of `fnox.toml`. With it the task fails (rc 1).
  - `fnox set` on an age provider stores ciphertext. Global fnox config
    `~/.config/fnox/config.toml` loads from any directory (currently
    `default_provider = "keychain"` plus one example secret).
  - Not tested: a root-owned target (cloudflared) through mise's sudo
    helper, and `--prompt-secrets` (needs a TTY).
  - Still to decide: provider (age recommended over keychain, since
    keychain needs an unlocked desktop session), where the real
    `fnox.toml` lives (versioned), and how interactive-shell secrets (the
    old atuin tokens) are handled: `fnox exec` per command or
    `fnox activate`.

Deploy, track, and sync dotfiles

A `[dotfiles]` entry deploys a file (from a source with `symlink`,
`symlink-each`, `copy`, or `template`, or from inline `content`), removes one
(`mode = "absent"`), sets an existing path's `permissions`, edits part of a
file, or tracks a live file where it is (`mode = "track"`). mise saves tracked
files to a local Git history that you can browse and roll back, and syncs it
with other machines through an origin repository. `mise dot` is a shorter alias.

Deploy files with `add`, `apply`, `diff`, `status`, and `unapply`. Track and
restore files with `track`, `save`, `history`, `rollback`, and `undo`. Sync them
with `origin`, `sync`, and `pull`.

See https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html and
https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles/history.html

Usage: mise dotfiles [--local] <SUBCOMMAND>

Commands:
  add        Start deploying a file, or copy its edits back to the source
  apply      Link, copy, and render `[dotfiles]` entries into place
  capture    Run a command and save tracked files before and after it
  conflicts  Compare both sides of a sync conflict
  diff       Show what `mise dot apply` would change
  edit       Open a dotfile's source in your editor
  exclude    Never save paths matching a glob
  history    Browse saved versions of your tracked files
  include    Stop excluding paths matching a glob
  notify     Send a test desktop notification
  origin     Show, connect, or disconnect the origin repository
  paths      List tracked paths and how they are saved
  pull       Write fetched changes from other machines to tracked files
  recover    Recover an interrupted dotfile operation
  rollback   Return files to the version a checkpoint holds
  save       Save a checkpoint of the tracked files now
  status     Show the state of your dotfiles and their history [aliases: ls]
  sync       Push saved checkpoints and fetch incoming changes
  track      Track a file or directory in place
  unapply    Remove files that `mise dot apply` deployed
  undo       Reverse the tracked-file changes from an operation

# tmux

Personal changes on top of Omarchy's shipped tmux config
(`~/.local/share/omarchy/config/tmux/tmux.conf`). Lives in
`~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf`. Anything not listed here is Omarchy's default.

Prefix is Omarchy's (`C-Space`).

## Changes from Omarchy defaults

| Keys                 | Omarchy default        | Personal                     |
|----------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| `prefix -` / `prefix \|` | —                  | Split stacked / side by side |
| `prefix h` / `prefix v`  | Split stacked / side by side | (freed; `h` is previous window) |
| `M-hjkl`             | —                      | Focus pane left/down/up/right |
| `C-M-arrows`         | Focus pane             | (unbound)                    |
| `M-HJKL`             | —                      | Resize pane left/down/up/right by 5 |
| `C-M-S-arrows`       | Resize pane            | (unbound)                    |
| `prefix h` / `prefix l` | —                   | Previous / next window       |

hjkl follows the same left/down/up/right convention as the window manager
(see @window-manager.md), so focus and resize use the same keys one layer
down, with Alt instead of Super.

## Keeping it

`omarchy-refresh-config tmux/tmux.conf` (and the 2026-10-25 04:00 reset,
mise checkpoint 569) replaces the file with the stock version. Check with:

```sh
diff ~/.local/share/omarchy/config/tmux/tmux.conf ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf
```

The diff should show exactly the rows above. Anything less means a refresh
ran; restore from `mise dot history` (see @mise.md).

# herdr
-herdr (https://herdr.dev) is a terminal workspace manager for coding agents:
-workspaces, tabs and panes, with agent state (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`,

# herdr

herdr (https://herdr.dev) is a terminal workspace manager for coding agents:
workspaces, tabs and panes, with agent state (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`,
`done`) recognised per pane. It is how skogai's agents get visible panes
and can drive each other. This page records the setup and the conventions
agreed for skogai; the binary's own `herdr --skill` is the authority on
command syntax.

## Per-machine setup

- Binary: `/usr/bin/herdr` (0.9.3 at time of writing). Server runs under
  the user; the socket is `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`.
- Config: `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`. It mirrors the Omarchy tmux config
  (`prefix = ctrl+space`, `prefix+c` new tab, `alt+h/j/k/l` focus). Apply
  changes with `herdr server reload-config`.
- Shell: `dash-skogai/fish/config.fish` loads `herdr completion fish`.
- Window manager: Omarchy's "Herdr" floating terminal is the dropdown
  terminal on `Mod+grave` (see `window-manager.md`).

## Agent integration

Claude Code reports pane state through a hook, installed by herdr:

- Hook: `~/.claude/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh`, a symlink directory to
  `/skogai/scripts/claude/hooks/`. The file is herdr-managed and is
  overwritten by `herdr integration install claude`.
- Settings: `~/.claude/settings.json` runs it with `session` on hooks.
- Check: `herdr integration status`. Upgrade the Claude hook with
  `herdr integration install claude` (v8 → v10 on 2026-10-07).

Other agents on this machine, as of the same check: pi and opencode are
outdated (`herdr integration install pi` / `opencode`); codex and hermes are
current; the rest are not installed.

## Conventions for skogai

- Agents act on herdr only from inside a herdr pane. The check is
  `test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1`. Outside herdr, do not control the focused
  session.
- Target panes by the IDs returned from JSON (`.result.pane.pane_id`), by
  `--current`, or by a unique live agent name. Never by sidebar order or
  a focused pane that may belong to the user.
- New work goes into a sibling pane in the caller's tab, in the caller's
  cwd, with `--no-focus`. Workspaces, tabs and worktrees are only created
  when asked for.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes or sessions that the agent did not
  create. Never run `herdr server stop` from inside an active session.
- Prompt an agent with `herdr agent prompt <name> "<text>" --wait`. If it
  returns `blocked`, read it with `herdr agent read` and ask the user before
  answering an approval dialog. Do not resubmit a prompt after a timeout
  without checking; it may have been delivered.
- Experiments that need their own server use `--session <name>`, not the
  main session.

## Open

- Whether skogai coordination (`gptme-coordination`) should write
  herdr pane names, so a task's agent can be found by name.
- Whether the `herdr` skill (`herdr --skill`) should be installed as a
  Claude skill for skogai agents, instead of being read on demand.

# herdr

herdr (https://herdr.dev) is a terminal workspace manager for coding agents:
workspaces, tabs and panes, with agent state (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`,
`done`) recognised per pane. It is how skogai's agents get visible panes
and can drive each other. This page records the setup and the conventions
agreed for skogai; the binary's own `herdr --skill` is the authority on
command syntax.

## Per-machine setup

- Binary: `/usr/bin/herdr` (0.9.3 at time of writing). Server runs under
  the user; the socket is `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`.
- Config: `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`, Omarchy's shipped config plus the
  personal changes under "Keybindings" below. Apply changes with
  `herdr server reload-config`.
- Shell: `dash-skogai/fish/config.fish` loads `herdr completion fish`.
- Window manager: Omarchy's "Herdr" floating terminal is the dropdown
  terminal on `Mod+grave` (see `window-manager.md`).

## Agent integration

Claude Code reports pane state through a hook, installed by herdr:

- Hook: `~/.claude/hooks/herdr-agent-state.sh`, a symlink directory to
  `/skogai/scripts/claude/hooks/`. The file is herdr-managed and is
  overwritten by `herdr integration install claude`.
- Settings: `~/.claude/settings.json` runs it with `session` on hooks.
- Check: `herdr integration status`. Upgrade the Claude hook with
  `herdr integration install claude` (v8 → v10 on 2026-10-07).

Other agents on this machine, as of the same check: pi and opencode are
outdated (`herdr integration install pi` / `opencode`); codex and hermes are
current; the rest are not installed.

## Conventions for skogai

- Agents act on herdr only from inside a herdr pane. The check is
  `test "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1`. Outside herdr, do not control the focused
  session.
- Target panes by the IDs returned from JSON (`.result.pane.pane_id`), by
  `--current`, or by a unique live agent name. Never by sidebar order or
  a focused pane that may belong to the user.
- New work goes into a sibling pane in the caller's tab, in the caller's
  cwd, with `--no-focus`. Workspaces, tabs and worktrees are only created
  when asked for.
- Do not close workspaces, tabs, panes or sessions that the agent did not
  create. Never run `herdr server stop` from inside an active session.
- Prompt an agent with `herdr agent prompt <name> "<text>" --wait`. If it
  returns `blocked`, read it with `herdr agent read` and ask the user before
  answering an approval dialog. Do not resubmit a prompt after a timeout
  without checking; it may have been delivered.
- Experiments that need their own server use `--session <name>`, not the
  main session.

## Open

- Whether skogai coordination (`gptme-coordination`) should write
  herdr pane names, so a task's agent can be found by name.
- Whether the `herdr` skill (`herdr --skill`) should be installed as a
  Claude skill for skogai agents, instead of being read on demand.

# tmux

Personal changes on top of Omarchy's shipped tmux config
(`~/.local/share/omarchy/config/tmux/tmux.conf`). Lives in
`~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf`. Anything not listed here is Omarchy's default.

Prefix is Omarchy's (`C-Space`).

## Changes from Omarchy defaults

| Keys                 | Omarchy default        | Personal                     |
|----------------------|------------------------|------------------------------|
| `prefix -` / `prefix \|` | —                  | Split stacked / side by side |
| `prefix h` / `prefix v`  | Split stacked / side by side | (freed; `h` is previous window) |
| `M-hjkl`             | —                      | Focus pane left/down/up/right |
| `C-M-arrows`         | Focus pane             | (unbound)                    |
| `M-HJKL`             | —                      | Resize pane left/down/up/right by 5 |
| `C-M-S-arrows`       | Resize pane            | (unbound)                    |
| `prefix h` / `prefix l` | —                   | Previous / next window       |

hjkl follows the same left/down/up/right convention as the window manager
(see @window-manager.md), so focus and resize use the same keys one layer
down, with Alt instead of Super.

## Keeping it

`omarchy-refresh-config tmux/tmux.conf` (and the 2026-10-25 04:00 reset,
mise checkpoint 569) replaces the file with the stock version. Check with:

```sh
diff ~/.local/share/omarchy/config/tmux/tmux.conf ~/.config/tmux/tmux.conf
```

The diff should show exactly the rows above. Anything less means a refresh
ran; restore from `mise dot history` (see @mise.md).

You don't make commits with `mise dot`. mise saves versions on its own, and the origin is just a shared copy of those versions for your other machines.

## On one machine

- **Store:** `~/.local/state/mise/history/repo.git` is an ordinary git repo, but only mise writes to it. Never run raw git on it.
- **Checkpoints:** a checkpoint is one commit holding every tracked file. They're created three ways:
  - the watcher (`dev.mise.mise-history`) saves one when a tracked file changes, at most once every 24h for files that change often, like `mise/config.toml`;
  - `mise dot save` saves one by hand;
  - every operation that writes tracked files (`bootstrap`, `pull`, `rollback`, `undo`, `apply`) saves one first, before writing anything.
- **Going back:**
  - `mise dot rollback <path> [--to N]` restores a single file;
  - `mise dot undo [N]` reverses one whole operation, such as a bad pull or bootstrap;
  - `mise dot history ls / show / diff` browses the history;
  - `mise dot history describe N` gives a checkpoint a meaningful name (messages are automatic otherwise).

## Between machines (origin)

- **Origin:** set with `mise dot origin set <url>`. It's one repo and one branch shared by every machine. Yours is `skogai2/.dotfiles` on `main`, declared in `config.local.toml`.
- **`sync`** pushes your checkpoints and fetches theirs. It never changes your files.
- **`pull`** writes what was fetched. It refuses if a file has unsaved edits or changed on both sides.
- **Conflicts:** a file that changed on both sides is a conflict, and it blocks pushing and applying for everything until you resolve it: `mise dot conflicts` to compare, then `pull --keep-local` or `pull --take-remote`.
- **Your mode is `sync`,** so the watcher syncs and pulls on its own whenever there are no conflicts. Day to day you do nothing, and `mise dot status` is the place to check.
- **New machine:** `mise bootstrap --adopt skogai2/.dotfiles` clones the history and writes the files. Because `~/.config/mise` is tracked, `config.toml` comes along with them, and the same bootstrap then applies packages, accounts, repos and so on.

## How it differs from your git repos

| | `~/.config/skogai`, `/skogai`, … | `mise dot` history |
|---|---|---|
| Commits | deliberate, with a message | automatic snapshots |
| Unit | one repo | every tracked path, as one snapshot |
| Branches | yes | no, one branch shared by all machines |
| Owner | you | mise |

mise records each decision and applies the incoming files only once every
conflict is resolved. It checks the plan again before it continues, and a
newer local or remote edit can cancel a decision, in which case you choose
again.

batch; `mise dot status` and `mise doctor` name the paths and the last
successful application. A few conflicts cannot be resolved with `pull`, such

histories with several Git merge bases. For those, `status` prints Git

## How the upstream flow behaves

| What the agent pushes | What the machine does |
|---|---|
| An edit to a tracked file | Written on the next sync/pull. The commit message becomes the checkpoint description. |
| A new file in a tracked directory | Created. |
| A file under a path that isn't tracked | **Ignored, with no warning.** |
| A new `[dotfiles]` entry in `config/config.toml` plus the file | The config arrives first and the file on the next round. The watcher handles both by itself. |
| A README or other notes | Stay in git and never land on the machine. A README is a good place for agent guidance. |
| The same file edited locally too | A whole-file conflict with no line merge. Sharing stops for every file until someone picks a side. |

## two ways to change a dotfile

- **live, on this machine:** edit the file in `~`. The watcher saves a

  machine pulls it. For prepared changes, changes meant for several

```tree
├── home/           # tracked files, as paths under ~ (live on every machine)
├── config/         # ~/.config/mise: config.toml, files/ (live)
├── .mise-history/  # mise's own; never edit
├── .skogai/        # agent environment: helpers, notes, drafts (never live)
└── README.md       # route for whoever checks the repo out (never live)
```

disk (tested 2026-10-25). That makes the origin a workspace for agents:

changing any machine.

# Atuin

Atuin (https://atuin.sh) is installed and is Emil's primary way of both
storing shell history and managing environment variables/aliases across
machines. This is a living record of that setup, updated directly as the
agreement changes — not derived from any single dotfiles file.

## What it does here

- **Shell history sync.** Every command run in an interactive shell is
  recorded and synced to Emil's atuin.sh account (username `skogix`), so
  history is shared across machines.
- **Env vars and aliases.** New environment variables and shell aliases are
  added via Atuin's dotfiles feature, not hand-written into `.bashrc`/`.zshrc`,
  so they sync to every machine automatically:
  - `atuin dotfiles var set NAME=value` — add/update an env var
  - `atuin dotfiles var delete NAME` — remove one
  - `atuin dotfiles var list` — see what's set
  - `atuin dotfiles alias set name=command` — add/update an alias
  - `atuin dotfiles alias delete name` / `list` / `clear` — same idea

  Only truly machine-local, one-off values (things that must never sync)
  belong directly in shell rc files instead.

- Package: `atuin` (Arch `extra` repo).

===== containers.md (120 lines)
# Containers: Docker → Podman

This is a living record of the container-runtime setup, updated directly as
the agreement changes — not derived from any single dotfiles file. It
documents a deliberate divergence from Omarchy's stock Docker setup, the same
way `window-manager.md` tracks divergence from Omarchy's default bindings.

## Why

Omarchy ships a full Docker environment by default: `docker`,
`docker-buildx`, `docker-compose`, `lazydocker`, `ufw-docker`, a `docker.socket`
enabled at boot, Docker-specific UFW rules, a `Super+Shift+D` TUI binding, a
Docker.desktop launcher, and menu entries — plus an opt-in (never used on this
machine) "Sudoless Docker" toggle that adds the user to the root-equivalent
`docker` group. Emil decided to move off Docker entirely in favor of Podman
(rootless by default, no always-on root daemon) rather than keep tuned the
sudoless-vs-sudo Docker tradeoff.

## What changes

- **Packages:** remove `docker`, `docker-compose`, `docker-buildx`,
  `ufw-docker`. Install `podman`, `podman-docker` (provides/conflicts with
  `docker` — this is what lets the `docker` command keep working, backed by
  Podman), `podman-compose`.
- **`lazydocker` stays installed.** It has no hard dependency on the `docker`
  package. It talks to the Docker Engine API at `$DOCKER_HOST`, which
  `podman-docker` points at the rootless Podman socket (see the systemd
  bullet), so it keeps working as long as `podman.socket` is enabled.
- **No changes needed to:** `~/.config/hypr` (`Super+Shift+D` binding),
  Docker.desktop launcher, Omarchy menu entries, or the `d=docker` atuin
  alias — all of them call `docker`, which keeps working.
- **systemd:** disable/stop `docker.socket`. Podman doesn't need an
  always-on root daemon. The `podman` CLI itself (`podman ps`, quadlets,
  `podman-compose`) is daemonless and reads container state directly, with
  no socket involved. Docker-API clients are different: lazydocker, Docker
  SDKs, and anything that mounts `docker.sock`. `podman-docker` ships
  `/etc/profile.d/podman-docker.sh`, which exports `DOCKER_HOST` to the
  rootless socket (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock`) for non-root
  users. So keep **`podman.socket` (user-level) enabled**. It starts
  `podman.service` on demand; don't enable the service itself (step 9).

# herdr

herdr (https://herdr.dev) is a terminal workspace manager for coding agents:
workspaces, tabs and panes, with agent state (`idle`, `working`, `blocked`,
`done`) recognised per pane. It is how skogai's agents get visible panes
and can drive each other. This page records the setup and the conventions
agreed for skogai; the binary's own `herdr --skill` is the authority on
command syntax.

## Per-machine setup

- Binary: `/usr/bin/herdr` (0.9.3 at time of writing). Server runs under
  the user; the socket is `~/.config/herdr/herdr.sock`.
- Config: `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`, Omarchy's shipped config plus the
  personal changes under "Keybindings" below. Apply changes with
  `herdr server reload-config`.
- Shell: `dash-skogai/fish/config.fish` loads `herdr completion fish`.
- Window manager: Omarchy's "Herdr" floating terminal is the dropdown
  terminal on `Mod+grave` (see `window-manager.md`).

## Keybindings

Changes on top of Omarchy's shipped config
(`~/.local/share/omarchy/config/herdr/config.toml`). Anything not listed is
Omarchy's default. Omarchy's herdr config mirrors its tmux config
(session -> workspace, window -> tab, pane -> pane), and the personal keys
mirror @tmux.md the same way. Prefix is `ctrl+space`.

# Secrets: keys and who can read what

A living record of how secrets are encrypted and which user can decrypt
them, updated directly as the agreement changes. **Status: draft
(2026-10-14).** Nothing below has been created on the machine yet. The
mise side (how secrets reach `mise bootstrap` and tasks) is in `mise.md`,
item 4.

## Model

- Secrets are stored with fnox, encrypted with age. `fnox.toml` holds only
  ciphertext, so it is safe to commit and to share between users.
- A secret is encrypted to a list of **recipients** (public keys). Any one
  matching **identity** (private key) decrypts it.
- Separation between users comes from Linux file permissions on the
  identity files, not from fnox profiles. A profile only chooses which
  secrets get asked for.
- Trust goes one way: skogix (the admin, with sudo) can reach everything;
  agents can reach only their own keys.

## Keys

| File | Owner, mode | Created by | Leaves the machine | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `~skogix/.ssh/skogix-age.txt` | skogix, 0600 | skogix, once | Yes, carried like `id_rsa` | Personal and admin key: reads everything, enrols new keys |
| `~skogix/.ssh/local-per-machine-age.txt` | skogix, 0600 | bootstrap task, if missing | Never | skogix on this machine; revoke one machine on its own |
| `~claude/.ssh/local-per-machine-age.txt` | claude, 0600 | bootstrap task (as claude), if missing | Never | claude on this machine |

`~skogix/.ssh` and `~claude/.ssh` are 0700 and owned by their user. The
other agents (dot, amy, goose) follow the claude row when they need keys.

## Providers and profiles

Two fnox ideas that are easy to mix up (and were, in the Oct 11 tests):

- A **provider** decides how a secret is encrypted. For age that is the
  recipient list, so it decides **who can decrypt**. Providers are named

# Window manager

This is a living record of the window-manager conventions Emil and Claude
have agreed on, updated directly as that agreement changes. It is not
derived from, or synced against, any single dotfiles config — if a machine's
actual config drifts from this file, that's a prompt to reconcile the two in
conversation, not to treat the dotfiles as authoritative.

## Base layout

- Layout: `se` (Swedish), variant `us_dvorak`, option `caps:swapescape`
- Applies across machines — every binding below assumes physical `hjkl`
  sits wherever Dvorak puts those letters, not where US QWERTY would.

Mod key is Super (Mod4).

| Keys                          | Action                                     |
|--------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| `Mod+Return`                   | Terminal                                    |
| `Mod+Shift+Return`             | Browser                                     |
| `Mod+d`                        | App launcher (Apps menu)                    |
| `Mod+hjkl`                     | Focus left/down/up/right window or group    |
| `Mod+Shift+hjkl`               | Move window or group left/down/up/right     |
| `Mod+t`                        | Window-group toggle (stacking) — i3's split v/h and layout-cycle keys are folded into this one toggle; `Mod+v`/`Mod+b` are retired |
| `Mod+f`                        | Fullscreen toggle                           |
| `Mod+Shift+Space`              | Floating toggle                             |

| `Mod+Ctrl+Left/Right`          | Previous/next workspace                     |
| `Mod+Ctrl+h/l`                 | Previous/next workspace (h/l mirror)        |
| `Mod+Shift+Ctrl+Left/Right`    | Move window or group to prev/next workspace, follow |

> in other words we can essentially build agent-environment, helpers and so on, in the dotfiles repo itself. and if not actively added as dotfiles they wouldn't even affect the machine itself. if so, could we get a basic workflow created for how we should do changes in this manner?

**Assistant**

Yes. You can build agent tooling inside the dotfiles repo, and nothing outside `home/` and `config/` ever reaches a machine. A second container test confirmed it: the machine made 4 commits of its own (a bootstrap, a pull and a local edit) and pushed them, and `README.md` and `.skogai/helpers/` survived every one without being written to `~`.

The workflow is in `dotfiles.md`, linked from `SKOGAI.md` (commit `25aa95b`):

- **Two ways to change things:**
  - **Live:** edit the file in `~` and the watcher saves and syncs it.
  - **Upstream:** clone the origin, commit, push, and every machine pulls it.
- **Origin layout:** `home/` and `config/` are live. `.skogai/` holds the agent environment, helpers and drafts, and is never live. `README.md` is the guide for whoever checks the repo out.
- **Steps:**
  1. Pull just before starting.
  2. Edit under `home/`, or add a `[dotfiles]` entry in `config/config.toml` to make a new path live.
  3. Make one commit per change, with a message that reads well in `mise dot history ls`.
  4. `git pull --rebase`, then push. Never force-push.
- **Making a draft live:** move it from `.skogai/` into `home/`, adding the `[dotfiles]` entry if the path is new. That single commit is when it starts affecting machines.
- **Don't park drafts under `home/` on an untracked path.** Declaring that path later would suddenly make them live.
- **No secrets in hand-made commits.** mise's secret check only runs inside its own commands, so a plain `git push` skips it.

The real origin doesn't have a `README.md` or `.skogai/` yet. Pushing a short README that points to this workflow would be the first real run of it. It's a push to GitHub, so shall I do it?

- Bash: `S=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-skogix--config-skogai/42b0c1bc-08cc-47c5-b006-de80818fdcaa/scratchpad; cd $S; rm -rf origin.git…`
- Bash: `podman exec mise-adopt-test su - tester -c 'mise dot sync -v 2>&1 | grep -iE "error|refus|reject|cannot" | head; mise do…`
- Bash: `S=/tmp/claude-1000/-home-skogix--config-skogai/42b0c1bc-08cc-47c5-b006-de80818fdcaa/scratchpad; chmod -R a+rwX $S/origin…` (failed)
- Write `dotfiles.md`
- Bash: `podman rm -f -t 0 mise-adopt-test >/dev/null; cd ~/.config/skogai; cat SKOGAI.md | sed -n 1,8p`
- Bash: `cd ~/.config/skogai; python3 -I - <<'EOF'`

# skogai config

How the machines skogai works on are configured, and the knowledge
behind that configuration. It's written for agents first: what each
part of the setup is, why it was chosen, and how to change it safely.

This repo holds no dotfiles and no machine state of its own. They
live where the tools that own them put them. This repo describes them
and routes to them.

## what is where

| what | where | versioned by |
|---|---|---|
| dotfiles (`~/.config/<app>/`) | in place, tracked by path rules | `mise dotfiles` history, synced to a private origin |
| machine state (packages, users, files, services, repos) | `~/.config/mise/config.toml` (`[bootstrap]`) | the same dotfiles history |
| knowledge, decisions, conventions | this repo, one page per concern | git |
| secrets | fnox + age (in progress) | ciphertext only |

## the base

- **mise** is the base: `mise dotfiles` tracks `~/.config`, and
  `mise bootstrap` declares and converges machine state. skogai builds
  on top of them and replaces neither.
- Each tool owns its own area (atuin: shell history, herdr: agent
  workspaces, podman: containers, Omarchy: the base system). skogai adds
  routes and conventions on top and doesn't reinvent any of them.

## pages

- `SKOGAI.md`: the root router; start here
- `PROJECT.md`: the current version's goals and plan
- `mise.md`: the mise walkthrough, decisions per feature
- `dotfiles.md`: how dotfiles change, live or upstream
- `secrets.md`, `atuin.md`, `containers.md`, `herdr.md`: one concern each
- `mappings.md`: keybindings (window manager, tmux, herdr)

## working here

- Read the page for a concern before changing anything in it. A page
  that contradicts the machine is wrong and gets fixed in the same turn.
- Read-only commands (`status`, `plan`, `diff`, `ls`, `--dry-run`) run
  freely. Anything that writes to the machine or pushes somewhere is
  confirmed first.
- Never read secret values into a conversation (`mise env`, `fnox get`,
  env files).

The first step of 3.0 (see SKOGAI.md, history).

- **mise is the base.** `mise dotfiles` tracks `~/.config` in place and
  `mise bootstrap` declares machine state. skogai builds on top of them
  and replaces neither.

  way stow did it.

  has skogai knowledge gets its own `SKOGAI.md`, versioned and synced
  with the app's config by mise history. Include-only dirs (fnox, herdr)
  need it added to their include list.

  tool.** For example `./secrets/{fnox,ssh,ssh-agent,mise}/`:
  `secrets/fnox/` holds most of the knowledge and tooling for fnox, and
  `secrets/mise/` the secret-specific part of mise (`mise secrets`).
- **`~/.config/skogai/SKOGAI.md` is the root router** for all skogai
  configuration.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Tests for shell/health: atuin sync freshness.
set -u

# shellcheck source=tests/lib.sh
source "$(dirname "$0")/lib.sh"

# atuin_case <status-out> <status-rc>: run shell/health with a stub atuin
# answering `status`.
atuin_case() {
  local d
  d=$(mktemp -d "$work/atuin.XXXX")
  printf '%s\n' "$1" >"$d/status.out"; echo "$2" >"$d/status.rc"
  # shellcheck disable=SC2016 # the body is a script; it expands when the stub runs
  stub "$d/bin" atuin '
case "$*" in
  status) s=status ;;
  *) exit 99 ;;
esac
cat "$STUB/$s.out"
exit "$(cat "$STUB/$s.rc")"'
  run env STUB="$d" PATH="$d/bin:$(toolbox)" "$repo/shell/health"
}

# synced <hours-ago>: a `Last sync:` line in atuin's format, in local time.
synced() {
  date -d "-$1 hours" '+Last sync: %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.347674749 %:z:00'
}

test_sync() {
  atuin_case "$(printf 'Atuin v18\n\n[Local]\n%s\n' "$(synced 3)")" 0
  expect "atuin: recent sync ok" 0 "ok atuin-sync: 3h ago"
  atuin_case "$(synced 30)" 0
  expect "atuin: stale sync fails" 1 "FAIL atuin-sync: last sync 30h ago"
  atuin_case "$(synced 24)" 0
  expect "atuin: exactly at the limit fails" 1 "FAIL atuin-sync: last sync 24h ago"
  atuin_case "Last sync: never" 0
  expect "atuin: unparseable sync line" 1 "FAIL atuin-sync: no Last sync: line"
  atuin_case "$(synced 1)" 2
  expect "atuin: status exit wins" 1 "FAIL atuin-sync: atuin status exited 2"
}

test_missing() {
  run env PATH="$(toolbox)" "$repo/shell/health"
  expect "atuin: not on PATH" 1 "FAIL atuin-sync: atuin not found"
  refute "atuin: no atuin-vars check" "atuin-vars"
}

test_sync
test_missing

exit $failures

# Context Summary

Persistent record of architectural decisions, discovered patterns, gotchas, and active context.
This file is referenced in CLAUDE.md and loaded every session.

## Active Context
- Done 2026-11-06: F001-F007. `bin/health` covers all 7 groups (16 checks); timer units in
- Coverage 2026-11-06 late: 3 undecided left (nvim.backup merge, pangolin, treehouse: skogix)
  `machine/units/` (not installed); `bin/check-coverage` + `mise/coverage.md`
- Next up: skogix's calls on the 4 live health failures and installing the timer; then
  work the 66 undecided `~/.config` entries into mise/coverage.md (PROJECT.md section 2)

## Cross-Cutting Concerns
- Stack: Markdown docs, plus bash checks in `bin/` and `tests/`
- Architecture: this repo is the root router for skogai config. Pages are
  grouped by concern (`secrets/`, `shell/`, `containers/`, `desktop/`,
  `agents/`, `mise/`), each group has a `SKOGAI.md` router. The dotfiles
  themselves live in `~/.config` and are versioned by mise history, not here.
- Key constraints:
  - mise's own commands on the dotfile history, never raw git on its store
  - read-only commands run freely; anything writing to the machine is confirmed
  - never read secret values into a conversation
  - one command per Bash call

## Domain: config knowledge

### Decisions
- Knowledge lives in this repo; `~/.config/<app>/SKOGAI.md` only routes back (2026-11-01)
- `mise/` stays one group until it's split into modules (2026-11-01)
- `full_test` = `tests/*.test.sh` + `bin/check-routes`: a route is a "- " line inside a
  `<routes>` block; prose mentions of files are not routes (2026-11-02)
- Push over HTTPS via `gh` (account Skogix); there's no SSH key for github.com (2026-11-02)
- Health checks: one executable `<group>/health` per concern, printing `ok|FAIL <check>[: detail]`
  lines; `bin/health` runs them all plus check-routes. A new concern joins by adding one file.
  On demand only for now; timer later (skogix, 2026-11-06)
- Concern health scripts source `bin/health-lib.sh` (report/need/tilde/join/stock_check);
  test files source `tests/lib.sh` (run/expect/refute/stub/toolbox) (2026-11-06)
- `bin/check-coverage` stays out of bin/health until section 2 is worked through; only
  skogix's decisions go in mise/coverage.md (2026-11-06)
- Commits carry no Co-Authored-By (decision 2026-10-30, `.skogai/handover.md`)

### Patterns
- every `mise dot` write goes through the lead, one at a time; agents return a verdict
  plus the exact command (handover 2026-10-30)

### Gotchas
- Omarchy refreshes replace personal configs silently (tmux.conf on 2026-11-02 07:39, leaving
  `tmux.conf.bak.<epoch>`); `stock_check` catches a byte-identical copy (2026-11-06)
- the tool shell is zsh: `${PIPESTATUS[0]}` and `command -v -a` don't work in Bash calls (2026-11-06)
- `sed -E "s|a\|b||"`: with `|` as delimiter, `\|` is ambiguous; use `#` (2026-11-06)
- `mise doctor` exits 1 when it has problems, and its output includes env/settings: parse only the
  `N problem(s) found:` block, never print the rest (2026-11-06)
- a timed-out health script's children (e.g. `sleep`) keep a pipe open: capture concern output to
  a temp file, not `$(...)`, or `timeout` returns but the runner still waits (2026-11-06)
- the harness was used and removed in `~/skogai` (memory `probe-method-lessons`,
  2026-10-31): a spec gate proves a spec is testable, not that it's worth building.
  Ask "what changes in the world if this works" first

- `mise dot status` exits 0 while publishing fails; the error is a `✗ last error:` line under
  Repository. `dot-sync` in mise/health catches it (2026-11-06)
- mise's name-based credential filter misses keys inside ordinary config files (Moonlight.conf
- `jq paths(scalars)` skips null values: a key-name scan with it misses empty `*_api_key` fields
  (basic-memory, 2026-11-06). Grep the raw file for names instead (2026-11-06)
  `key=`); its publish check catches them, but only after they're in local history. Before
  tracking a new app dir, grep key names (`cut -d= -f1`) for key/cert/token (2026-11-06)

- Removing plaintext from mise history without `history purge` (mise < 2026.11): stop
  `dev.mise.mise-history.service`, move `main` back to the last published commit
  (`refs/remotes/origin/setup`), `mise dot save`, then `reflog expire` + `gc --prune=now`.
  The publish check stops at the first hit: scan every new file before syncing, or it takes
  one reset per secret (three on 2026-11-06). Each reset needs skogix's approval, and
  `--allow-plaintext-history` is skogix's to run, never an agent's (2026-11-06)
